passage:
I’m ten, and I still remember pushing into the canteen line on Friday. The bell for maths was about to ring, so I slid in between Aadhya and a Class 8 boy and held out my coins. Nobody spoke at first. Aadhya just looked at me. Then someone behind us said, “The line starts back there.”
My face went hot. Part of me wanted to shout that I was in a hurry, and part of me felt very small. The Class 8 boy shrugged, but I picked up my coins and walked to the back. I got my samosa late. The hungry feeling was gone by afternoon, but the other feeling stayed longer.
— Sarita

qa.q: Where did Sarita push into the line, and why?
qa.a: Sarita pushed into the canteen line because the bell for maths was about to ring.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when the heat rose in Sarita's face?
qa.a: It was a mix of defiance and guilt. Part of Sarita wanted to shout about the hurry, and part felt very small.

qa.q: What choice changed how the moment ended for Sarita?
qa.a: Walking to the back of the line instead of arguing let Sarita put things right, even though the samosa came late.

qa.q: How might Aadhya have felt when Sarita slid in?
qa.a: Aadhya may have felt annoyed or ignored. Aadhya did not speak but just looked at Sarita, which shows Aadhya noticed and did not like it.

grounding: Shows a child cutting a line in a hurry, feeling defiance and guilt, and reacting to how the others responded.

passage:
Note, Wednesday, Class 5. After games, Gautam stepped in front of three classmates at the water cooler and said, “Just one sip, I’ll miss my bus.” Two children groaned. A quiet girl at the back lowered her bottle and stared at the floor. Gautam saw their faces and went red. His arms crossed, and he looked ready to argue.
I did not scold him in front of the others. I walked over and said, “The line starts back there. What are you hurrying for?” He said he was afraid the bus would leave. He went to the end of the line, and afterwards he told the group he was sorry.
Tomorrow I will let the bus monitor call his row first if time worries him.
— Minakshi, class teacher

qa.q: What did Gautam say when he stepped in front of his classmates?
qa.a: He said, “Just one sip, I’ll miss my bus.”

qa.q: What was Gautam probably feeling as he stood with crossed arms and a red face?
qa.a: He was likely feeling defiant and embarrassed at once. He went red after seeing the faces around him, yet he still looked ready to argue.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Gautam go to the back of the line?
qa.a: The teacher spoke to him privately and asked what he was hurrying for instead of scolding him publicly, which let him say he was afraid of missing the bus.

qa.q: How might the quiet girl at the back have felt when Gautam stepped in?
qa.a: She may have felt unfairly overlooked but too shy to say anything. She lowered her bottle and stared at the floor instead of speaking up.

grounding: Shows a child cutting a line out of hurry, feeling defiance and guilt, and a teacher's calm response.

passage: The school canteen queue was twenty children long, and Disha had dance rehearsal in ten minutes. She spotted her friend Manoj near the front and slipped in beside him. 'Just holding a place,' she said loudly, to nobody. The boy behind Manoj, a Class 3 kid holding coins, looked at her with big eyes and said nothing. Manoj said, 'Disha, he's been waiting since the bell.' Her face went hot. For a second she wanted to say she was in a hurry and it didn't matter. Then she saw the little boy's coins, counted out carefully. She stepped back and said, 'Sorry, you go.' She reached rehearsal two minutes late, and the teacher let it go.

qa.q: How long was the canteen queue?
qa.a: Twenty children long.

qa.q: What did Disha feel when Manoj spoke up?
qa.a: A flash of guilt and embarrassment, her face hot, with a moment of wanting to defend herself.

qa.q: What helped Disha change course?
qa.a: Manoj naming it plainly, and Disha noticing the little boy's carefully counted coins, which made the unfairness real.

qa.q: What might the Class 3 boy have felt when Disha slipped in?
qa.a: Probably small and upset but too shy to speak, since he had waited since the bell.

grounding: A child in a hurry cuts a queue, feels a flash of guilt when a friend objects, and steps back.

passage: Monday: at the school bus stop, Baljeet ducked in front of three younger kids to grab the window seat. Nobody said anything, and he felt clever. Wednesday: he did it again. This time Saurabh, from the next class, said, 'Back of the line, Baljeet.' Baljeet shrugged. 'Who's going to make me?' He felt defiant, and a little sick. Friday: at the book fair, a bigger boy pushed right in front of Baljeet at the comics table and took the last copy he'd been waiting for. 'Hey! I was here first!' Baljeet shouted. The boy laughed and walked off. On the bus home, Baljeet waited at the back of the line and didn't say why.

qa.q: What did the bigger boy take at the book fair?
qa.a: The last copy of the comic Baljeet had been waiting for.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when Saurabh told him to go to the back?
qa.a: Defiant on the outside and a little sick inside, knowing it wasn't fair.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do next time he's in a hurry?
qa.a: Wait his turn, or politely ask the others if he can go ahead, instead of pushing in.

qa.q: How might the three younger kids have felt on Monday?
qa.a: Pushed aside and too small to object, probably annoyed or hurt when Baljeet took the window seat.

grounding: Over a week a child cuts a line with defiance, then feels how it lands when someone cuts in front of him.

passage: Saurabh, you pushed ahead at the cinema counter today, didn't you? Let your Raghav dadu tell you something. When I was ten, in Asansol, we queued every week for kerosene. One morning I was late for a cricket match, so I pushed in front of an old woman with a cane. I thought she wouldn't mind. She didn't say anything. She just looked at me, and the whole line went quiet. The shopkeeper served me, and I ran off with the can, feeling like a thief. At the match I dropped two easy catches. That evening I went back and carried her can home for her. She gave me a sweet and said, 'Next time, just ask.' I've never forgotten her face.

qa.q: What did young Raghav queue for every week?
qa.a: Kerosene.

qa.q: How did young Raghav feel running off with the can?
qa.a: Guilty, like a thief, after the old woman's look and the line going quiet.

qa.q: Which choice in the story shows young Raghav putting things right?
qa.a: Going back that evening to carry the old woman's can home, owning what he had done.

qa.q: What might the old woman have felt when young Raghav pushed in?
qa.a: Probably hurt and tired, but she chose silence and later kindness, telling him, 'Next time, just ask.'

grounding: A grandfather recalls cutting a line as a boy in a hurry and the guilt that followed when others reacted.

passage: The last bell had gone, rain was hammering the tin roof, and the queue for the one water cooler stretched past the notice board. Keerthana's van left in five minutes. She looked at the line: Class 3 kids, a boy with a cricket bat, her classmate Shreya near the front. Nobody would mind, surely. She slipped in beside Shreya and held her bottle under the tap. "Oi!" said a small girl behind. "We were all waiting!" Shreya didn't say anything, just looked at her, and that was worse. Keerthana's cheeks went hot. Half of her wanted to shout, "My van's leaving!" The other half pulled the bottle back. "Sorry. Go," she mumbled, and stepped aside, the half-filled bottle dripping.

qa.q: How long until Keerthana's van left?
qa.a: Her van left in five minutes.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Shreya looked at her without a word?
qa.a: She felt guilty and embarrassed, cheeks hot, torn between defending herself and stepping back.

qa.q: What could Keerthana try next time she is in a hurry?
qa.a: She could ask the line politely whether she might go first because her van is leaving, instead of slipping in.

qa.q: How did the small girl behind see Keerthana's push?
qa.a: To her it was simply unfair, because they had all been waiting in the rain too.

grounding: Shows a child pushing ahead in a queue because she is in a hurry, then feeling a flash of guilt at how others react.
